entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Meitoku
entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Keichō
entities.date_note: Nengō 1596-1615 spans Azuchi-Momoyama into early Edo.

entities.name: Legendary Age (Three Sovereigns & Five Emperors)
entities.summary: The sage-rulers of Chinese tradition, placed before the Xia: god-kings credited with agriculture, medicine, writing and silk, then five emperors held up for millennia as the model of virtuous rule.
entities.date_note: Traditional bounds, not findings. The tradition has no single canonical form — five different lists of the Three Sovereigns appear in Han-dynasty classics, and the Five Emperors have as many competing groupings. Fuxi and Shennong appear in every list of Sovereigns and are authored beneath; the third slot is variously Suiren, Nüwa, Zhurong, Gonggong or the Yellow Emperor, so it is described here rather than filled by picking one list.

caveats.text: These are mythological figures. The tradition is real and consequential; the rulers are not attested archaeologically.
The regnal dates were calculated by 17th-century Jesuits from Chinese chronicles, then adopted in China via Sun Yat-sen and the 1938 Cihai.

entities.search_phrase: Three Sovereigns Five Emperors Chinese mythology

entities.name: Shang Dynasty
entities.summary: First historically confirmed Chinese dynasty. Oracle bones; bronze ritual vessels.

entities.name: Zhou Dynasty
entities.summary: Longest dynasty in Chinese history. Split into Western and Eastern (Spring-Autumn + Warring States).

entities.name: Spring and Autumn Period
entities.summary: Time of Confucius and Laozi.

entities.name: Warring States Period
entities.summary: Seven kingdoms fought for supremacy; Hundred Schools of Thought.
entities.date_note: Warring States is a historiographic period that outlasted the nominal Eastern Zhou.

entities.name: Qin Dynasty
entities.summary: First unified imperial state.

entities.name: Qin Shi Huangdi
entities.summary: First Emperor of unified China. Standardized script, currency, and weights. Terracotta Army.

entities.name: Han Dynasty
entities.summary: Classical Chinese empire; namesake of the Han Chinese ethnicity.

entities.name: Emperor Wu
entities.summary: Made Confucianism the state ideology; opened the Silk Road via Zhang Qian.

entities.name: Eastern Han
entities.summary: Paper invented by Cai Lun (c. 105); Buddhism enters China.
entities.date_note: Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.

entities.name: Three Kingdoms
entities.summary: Wei, Shu, and Wu — the era of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

entities.name: Jin Dynasty
entities.date_note: Britannica gives 265 for the start; the one-year difference is a matter of whether the abdication or the enthronement is counted.
entities.summary: Briefly reunified China after the Three Kingdoms, then lost the north to steppe powers and fled south — the beginning of nearly three centuries of division.

name_forms.name: Chin
name_forms.note: Wade-Giles gives Chin for both this dynasty (晉) and the later Jurchen Jin (金), so it cannot tell them apart. The characters can.

entities.name: Northern and Southern Dynasties
entities.summary: Rival northern and southern courts, the north under non-Han dynasties that progressively adopted Chinese administration. Buddhism spread widely in both.

name_forms.name: Nan-Pei Ch'ao
name_forms.note: Hyphenation not confirmed against a primary romanisation table. Older literature often calls the era the Six Dynasties instead.

entities.name: Sui Dynasty
entities.summary: Reunified China after nearly four centuries of division and built the Grand Canal, at ruinous cost, in two generations.

entities.name: Tang Dynasty
entities.summary: Golden age of Chinese poetry and cosmopolitan trade.

entities.name: Empress Wu Zetian
entities.summary: Only woman to rule China as emperor in her own right.

entities.name: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms
entities.summary: Five short-lived dynasties in the north and roughly ten kingdoms in the south, between the Tang and the Song. Printing spread and paper money first appeared in this fragmentation, not in spite of it.

entities.name: Song Dynasty
entities.summary: Economic and technological golden age: printing, gunpowder, compass, paper money.

entities.name: Yuan Dynasty
entities.date_note: Yuan formally ended in 1368 when the Ming took Beijing; Huizong ruled from Mongolia until 1370 (Northern Yuan).
entities.summary: Mongol-ruled China under the descendants of Genghis Khan.

links.note: Mongol-ruled dynasty in China after the fragmentation of the unified empire.
Overthrown by the Ming, which claimed the Mandate of Heaven.

name_forms.name: Yüan
name_forms.note: Differs from Pinyin only by the umlaut, which older printing often dropped, so one book may use both spellings.

entities.name: Kublai Khan
entities.summary: Grandson of Genghis; founder of the Yuan Dynasty.
entities.date_note: Kublai was Great Khan from 1260; founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271.

entities.name: Ming Dynasty
entities.summary: Restored Han Chinese rule; Zheng He's voyages; Forbidden City built.

entities.name: Yongle Emperor
entities.summary: Commissioned Zheng He's treasure voyages; moved capital to Beijing.

entities.name: Qing Dynasty
entities.summary: Manchu-ruled last imperial dynasty.

entities.name: Kangxi Emperor
entities.summary: Longest-reigning Qing emperor; consolidated Manchu rule and expanded the empire.

entities.name: Qianlong Emperor
entities.summary: Cultural peak of the Qing; long reign ending in stagnation.

links.note: Regent for her six-year-old son from 1861, initially sharing the office with Ci'an.
Regent again for her adopted three-year-old nephew, sole holder of the office after Ci'an's death in 1881.

entities.name: Republic of China
entities.date_note: 1912-1949 is the mainland period, not an uncontested lifespan. Whether the Republic of China ended in 1949 is a live dispute in international law: the PRC holds that it did, Taiwan's government states it relocated and has governed there ever since, and a third position holds it was a government of the state of China rather than a state in its own right.

alternatives.label: Ongoing since 1912 (relocated to Taiwan in 1949)
alternatives.note: Taiwan's official position: the government relocated and has exercised jurisdiction continuously since.

alternatives.label: Ended 1 October 1949
alternatives.note: The PRC's formal position, that its proclamation brought the historical status of the ROC to an end.

caveats.text: Whether this entity still exists is disputed between two governments. The end date shown is the loss of the mainland, which is not the same claim as dissolution.

name_forms.name: Taiwan
name_forms.note: The everyday name since the government relocated. Using it as the state's name is itself a position in the dispute.

name_forms.name: Republican Era
name_forms.note: How the 1912-1949 mainland period is usually named in Chinese historiography.

entities.summary: Post-imperial China, ending on the mainland with the Communist victory in 1949; continues on Taiwan.

entities.name: People's Republic of China

name_forms.name: China
name_forms.note: The short form is not neutral: which state it denotes is the substance of the dispute recorded on the Republic of China.

entities.summary: Founded by Mao Zedong in 1949; the world's most populous state until 2023.

entities.name: Gojoseon
entities.date_note: The 2333 BCE start is the traditional Dangun foundation date, not an archaeological one; there is no material evidence for it. The 108 BCE end is the Han conquest and is secure.

caveats.text: The 2333 BCE founding comes from the Dangun myth. Historians of Korea treat it as legend: there is no archaeological and very little textual evidence.

entities.summary: The first Korean state in the traditional account, in the peninsula's northwest and southern Manchuria, ended by Han conquest in 108 BCE.

entities.name: Three Kingdoms of Korea
entities.summary: Goguryeo, Baekje, Silla.

entities.name: Unified Silla
entities.summary: Silla, allied with Tang China, defeated Baekje and Goguryeo and then turned on its ally, unifying most of the peninsula for the first time and presiding over a Buddhist cultural peak.

entities.name: Goryeo Dynasty
entities.summary: Origin of the name 'Korea'; celadon ceramics; movable metal type.

entities.name: Joseon Dynasty
entities.summary: Long-lived Confucian monarchy; Hangul script created under Sejong the Great.

entities.name: King Sejong the Great
entities.summary: Fourth king of Joseon; created Hangul and oversaw Korea's greatest era of scientific and cultural achievement.

entities.name: Japanese Colonial Rule
entities.summary: Japanese annexation of Korea (1910–1945); ended by WWII.

entities.name: Divided Korea
entities.date_note: The two states do not share a word for the nation they both claim. The North uses Joseon, the South uses Hanguk, and English flattens both to 'Korea', which conceals a disagreement rather than resolving it.

caveats.text: There is no neutral Korean term for the country. Choosing Joseon or Hanguk takes a side; English 'Korea' only looks neutral because it discards the distinction.

name_forms.name: Chosŏn
name_forms.note: The North's word for the nation.

name_forms.name: Hanguk
name_forms.note: The South's word for the same nation.

entities.summary: Postwar division into North and South Korea after the Korean War.

entities.name: Sumerian Early Dynastic
entities.summary: World's first cities: Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish.

entities.name: Gilgamesh (legendary)
entities.summary: Legendary king of Uruk; hero of the eponymous epic.

caveats.text: Probably a real king of Uruk early in the 3rd millennium BCE, but no historical evidence supports the exploits the epic describes.

entities.name: Akkadian Empire
entities.summary: First empire in world history.

entities.name: Sargon of Akkad
entities.summary: Founder of the Akkadian Empire; considered the first empire-builder in world history.

entities.name: Ur III (Neo-Sumerian)
entities.summary: The last Sumerian-speaking dynasty, which left the earliest surviving law code and an administrative archive of tens of thousands of tablets.

entities.name: Old Babylonian Empire
entities.date_note: Middle Chronology, like every date in this era and the Kassite era that follows it. The whole 2nd-millennium Mesopotamian sequence shifts together depending on which chronology is adopted; see Hammurabi's reign for the detail.
entities.summary: Amorite dynasty of Babylon; Hammurabi's law code.

entities.name: Hammurabi
entities.summary: Famous for the Code of Hammurabi, one of the earliest surviving law codes.
entities.date_note: These are Middle Chronology dates, which is the usual default but only one of four schemes in use. The High, Low and Ultra-Low chronologies place the same reign progressively later or earlier, across a spread of roughly 120 years. There is no independent dating here: the sequence rests on king-lists anchored to the Venus Tablet of Ammi-saduqa, whose observations are astronomically periodic and so fit several real years equally well.

alternatives.label: Low Chronology, c. 1728-1686 BC
alternatives.note: One of the lower readings of the same Venus observations.

caveats.text: Quoted almost everywhere as simply Hammurabi's dates. Sources differing by decades are usually not in error; they have chosen a different chronology.

entities.name: Kassite Babylon
entities.date_note: These are middle-chronology figures, the convention most used in scientific publication. Short or long chronology shifts both ends by decades. 1595 BCE is the Hittite sack of Babylon.
entities.summary: Four centuries of stable Babylonian rule under a dynasty of foreign origin, during which Babylon became a recognised great power in the diplomacy of the Late Bronze Age.

entities.name: Assyrian Empires
entities.summary: Ancient Mesopotamian empires that dominated the Near East in the Iron Age.

entities.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
entities.summary: Mass deportations as imperial policy; library of Nineveh.

entities.name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
entities.summary: Chaldean dynasty that overthrew Assyria; Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem in 587 BCE.

entities.name: Nebuchadnezzar II
entities.summary: Destroyed Jerusalem (587 BCE); traditional builder of the Hanging Gardens.

entities.name: Kingdoms of Israel and Judah
entities.summary: Iron Age Hebrew kingdoms.

entities.name: David
entities.summary: Traditional second king of Israel; united the northern and southern kingdoms.

entities.name: Solomon
entities.summary: Traditional builder of the First Temple in Jerusalem.

entities.name: Phoenician City-States
entities.summary: Independent Canaanite-speaking city-states on the Levantine coast, never politically unified.
entities.date_note: Previously ended at 539 BCE, the Persian conquest. That marks a change of imperial overlord rather than an end: under Achaemenid rule Tyre, Sidon and Byblos kept their own kings and fleets, Sidon revolted, and Tyre withstood Alexander for seven months. Homeland independence ends in 332 BCE with the fall of Tyre. The start is approximate and marks the Late Bronze Age Canaanite phase from which these cities emerge, not a founding.

alternatives.label: 539 BCE, the Persian conquest
alternatives.note: A change of overlord; the cities kept their kings for two more centuries.

caveats.text: Phoenicia is Greek. No native collective equivalent is known: people identified as Tyrian, Sidonian or Byblian.
Quinn argues a collective Phoenician identity is largely a modern construction; others treat Canaanite as the self-designation. The question is open.
Never a state, an empire or a confederation -- independent competing cities under shifting informal primacy.

name_forms.name: Phoenicia
name_forms.note: From Greek phoinix. The name a reader arrives with, and an outsider's.

name_forms.name: Canaanite
name_forms.note: The plausible self-term per the Met; Quinn rejects even this as a collective identity.

entities.name: Achaemenid Empire
entities.summary: First Persian empire; largest of its time.

entities.name: Cyrus II the Great
entities.summary: Founder of the Achaemenid Empire; freed the Jews from Babylonian exile.
entities.date_note: Cyrus II ruled Persia from 559, becoming founder of the Achaemenid empire in 550.

entities.name: Cambyses II
entities.summary: Conquered Egypt (525 BCE).

entities.name: Darius I the Great
entities.summary: Great organizer; built Persepolis; invaded Greece and lost at Marathon.

entities.name: Xerxes I
entities.summary: Led the second Persian invasion of Greece; lost at Salamis and Plataea.

entities.name: Darius III
entities.summary: Last Achaemenid; defeated by Alexander the Great.

entities.name: Seleucid Empire
entities.summary: Hellenistic successor state to Alexander's eastern conquests; the biggest single Diadochi kingdom.

entities.name: Parthian (Arsacid) Empire
entities.summary: Iranian empire that ruled Persia and Mesopotamia for four centuries; Rome's chief eastern rival.

entities.name: Sasanian Empire
entities.summary: Last pre-Islamic Persian empire; peer superpower of Rome/Byzantium.

entities.name: Shapur I
entities.summary: Captured Roman Emperor Valerian alive at Edessa (260 CE).

entities.name: Khosrow I Anushirvan
entities.summary: Golden-age king; legal and administrative reforms.

entities.name: Safavid Empire
entities.summary: Made Shia Islam the state religion.

entities.name: Qajar Dynasty

alternatives.label: From the start of Agha Mohammad Khan's unification campaign
alternatives.note: The date this dataset used before it was sourced.

alternatives.label: From Agha Mohammad Khan's coronation as shah

entities.date_note: Britannica dates the dynasty from 1794, when Agha Mohammad Khan eliminated his last rival. 1789 (campaign) and 1796 (coronation) are also used.
entities.summary: The dynasty that lost the Caucasus to Russia, granted the concessions that made Iran a field of Anglo-Russian competition, and was forced into a constitution in 1906.

entities.name: Pahlavi Dynasty
entities.summary: Last royal dynasty of Iran; overthrown by the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

entities.name: Islamic Republic of Iran
entities.summary: Theocratic state established by Ayatollah Khomeini after the 1979 revolution.

entities.name: Rise of Islam
entities.summary: Muhammad's prophetic career and the birth of Islam.

entities.name: Prophet Muhammad
entities.summary: Founder of Islam; united most of Arabia under his rule by 632.

entities.name: Rashidun Caliphate
entities.summary: First four 'rightly guided' caliphs; rapid conquest of Persia, Levant, and Egypt.

entities.name: Umayyad Caliphate
entities.summary: Dynasty ruling from Damascus. Reached from Iberia to Central Asia.

entities.name: Abbasid Caliphate
entities.summary: Ruled from Baghdad; Islamic Golden Age. Ended by Mongol sack of Baghdad.

links.note: Held Baghdad while the Fatimids claimed the same office from Cairo.

caveats.text: The four caliphates were not a clean succession: the Fatimids claimed the same office from Cairo for 262 years of Abbasid rule.

entities.name: Harun al-Rashid
entities.summary: Fifth Abbasid caliph; his court is the setting of many One Thousand and One Nights tales.

entities.name: Fatimid Caliphate
entities.summary: Isma'ili Shia caliphate; founded Cairo and Al-Azhar.

links.note: Claimed the caliphate as Ismaili Shia imams against the Abbasids in Baghdad.

entities.name: Ottoman Empire
entities.summary: Multi-continental empire spanning Anatolia, the Balkans, North Africa, and the Arab world.

name_forms.name: Devlet-i ʿAlīye-i ʿOsmānīye
name_forms.note: 'The Sublime Ottoman State'.

name_forms.name: Devlet-i Aliyye
name_forms.note: 'The Exalted State', used from the founding; 'Osmaniyye' was added during the Tanzimat.

name_forms.name: Turkish Empire
name_forms.note: The usual Western European name. The state did not call itself Turkish.

entities.name: Mehmed II the Conqueror
entities.summary: Conquered Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire.

entities.name: Suleiman I the Magnificent
entities.summary: Longest-reigning Ottoman sultan; peak of Ottoman power and cultural achievement.

entities.name: Ancient Greece
entities.date_note: Corrected from 3000 BCE, which was a rounding. The British Museum, Cambridge and Smarthistory all place the start of the Greek Bronze Age at about 3200 BC. Note the two ends are different kinds of date: a periodisation boundary at the start, and the Roman sack of Corinth in 146 BCE at the end.

caveats.text: A round 3000 BCE circulates widely for the start of Greek prehistory. It is a rounding of the 3200 BC convention, not a separate finding.

entities.summary: Cradle of Western philosophy, drama, historiography, and democracy.

entities.name: Minoan Civilization
entities.summary: Bronze Age Cretan civilization; palace at Knossos.

entities.name: Mycenaean Civilization
entities.date_note: 1600-1100 BC is the British Museum's convention and a defensible one, but not the only one: start dates of 1750, 1700 and 1675 BCE are all in print. The whole Aegean absolute chronology this sits inside is unresolved, because radiocarbon dating of the Thera eruption and the Egyptian synchronisms disagree by roughly a century.

alternatives.label: Aegean high chronology, from c. 1700 BCE
alternatives.note: Follows the radiocarbon dating of the Thera eruption rather than the Egyptian synchronisms, and pushes the Late Bronze Age Aegean about a century earlier.

caveats.text: Aegean Bronze Age dates are not independently fixed. They inherit the unresolved Thera dispute, which recent work has narrowed without settling.

entities.summary: Late Bronze Age Greek civilization; the world of Homer's epics.

entities.name: Greek Dark Ages

caveats.text: “Dark Age” is disputed and increasingly avoided. Protogeometric, Geometric and Early Iron Age are used instead; the period was not uniformly one of decline.

entities.summary: The centuries between the collapse of Mycenaean palace society and the emergence of the city-states: writing was lost and populations fell, but iron came into use and the epics took shape.

entities.name: Archaic Greece
entities.date_note: A modern retrospective label, coined in the 18th century, not a period the Greeks recognised. The end is usually pinned to the Persian Wars, which some schemes date to 479 rather than 480 BCE.
entities.summary: Formative period of the polis, colonization, and archaic art.

entities.name: Classical Greece
entities.summary: Age of Athens' Golden Age, the Peloponnesian War, and philosophers Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle.
entities.date_note: Bracketed by two attested events, the end of the Persian Wars and the death of Alexander in 323 BCE, but 'Classical' is itself a modern retrospective category rather than a contemporary one.

entities.name: Pericles (statesman)
entities.summary: Athenian statesman who led the city through its cultural Golden Age.

entities.name: Kingdom of Macedon
entities.date_note: Corrected from 808 BCE. Britannica, the Oxford Companion to Classical Literature and the Lexicon of Argead Macedonia all date the historically attested kingdom to about 700 BC under Perdiccas I. The end, Roman annexation in 146 BCE, is securely attested.

alternatives.label: Traditional foundation by Karanos, 808 BCE
alternatives.note: A king-list back-calculation to a founder ancient authors themselves disputed. Herodotus credits Perdiccas I instead and does not mention Karanos.

caveats.text: 808 BCE is still widely printed as Macedon's founding. It is legend systematised into a king-list, structurally the same as Rome's 753.

entities.summary: Northern Greek kingdom that under Philip II and Alexander conquered the classical world.

entities.name: Philip II of Macedon
entities.summary: Reorganized the Macedonian army and unified Greece under Macedonian hegemony.

entities.name: Alexander the Great
entities.summary: Conquered the Achaemenid Empire, reaching India. Ushered in the Hellenistic Age.

name_forms.name: Iskandar
name_forms.note: The Persian and later Islamic form, through which he entered a very different body of legend.

entities.name: Hellenistic Period
entities.date_note: From Alexander's death in 323 BCE to Actium in 31. The term was coined by Droysen in the 19th century; no one living through it called it that.
entities.summary: Age of Greek-influenced kingdoms from Alexander's death to Actium.

entities.name: Ancient Rome
entities.date_note: Both ends are conventions rather than facts. 753 BCE is Varro's back-calculation, which the Oxford Classical Dictionary calls artificial manipulation that does not accord with any archaeological starting point. 476 CE is Gibbon's marker, which Britannica declines to give at all, preferring 'the 5th century'.

alternatives.label: Ancient authors gave at least six founding years
alternatives.note: Timaeus 841, Polybius and Diodorus 750, Dionysius 751, Livy 749, Fabius Pictor 747, Cincius 728 BC. Varro's 753 won on authority, not evidence.

caveats.text: Settlement on the Palatine is attested well before 753 BCE and an urbanised city-state considerably after it. The traditional year matches neither.

entities.summary: From the legendary founding to the fall of the Western Empire; the political and cultural core of the ancient Mediterranean.

entities.name: Roman Kingdom
entities.summary: Seven legendary kings from Romulus to Tarquin the Proud.

entities.name: Roman Republic
entities.date_note: 509 BCE is the Varronian date and the Oxford Classical Dictionary describes the Varronian scheme as incorrect in places; modern scholarship generally prefers 508 or 507. The end, 27 BCE, is securely attested.

caveats.text: 509 BCE is a Varronian reckoning, not an attested year. The expulsion of the kings is not dated by any contemporary record.

entities.summary: Non-monarchical Rome governed by the Senate and elected magistrates.

entities.name: Late Republic
entities.date_note: A modern periodisation running from the tribunate of Tiberius Gracchus in 133 BCE. Its end is variously given as 44, 31 or 27 BCE depending on whether the marker is Caesar's death, Actium, or the settlement with the Senate.
entities.summary: Era of Marius, Sulla, Pompey, Caesar, and Octavian; ended by civil wars that produced the Empire.

entities.name: Julius Caesar
entities.summary: Dictator perpetuo; assassinated on the Ides of March, 44 BCE.

entities.name: Roman Empire
entities.date_note: The start is solid: the Senate granted Octavian the title Augustus on 16 January 27 BCE. The end is not. 476 CE is an 18th-century convention popularised by Gibbon, whose own footnote conceded the year is not positively ascertained, and a 2024 paper argues even the day is doubtful. Filed under Ancient Rome alongside the Kingdom and the Republic. It previously sat beside them as a sibling, which left the emperors unreachable from Rome by either search or drilling.

alternatives.label: Ends 480 CE, with Julius Nepos
alternatives.note: Nepos was the last legitimate western emperor and outlived Romulus Augustulus's deposition by four years.

alternatives.label: Ends 410 CE, with the sack of Rome
alternatives.note: One of several rival markers, alongside the Rhine crossing of 406 and the Vandal sack of 455.

caveats.text: A UCL thesis puts it plainly: 476 is not the year in which the empire ended, and never was. Britannica gives no year, only the 5th century.
"Roman Empire" means both the state from 27 BCE and the whole Roman epoch, as in The Rise and Fall of the Roman Empire. This is the state; the epoch is Ancient Rome, above.

entities.summary: Monarchical Roman state from Augustus's Principate to the deposition of Romulus Augustulus.

entities.name: Augustus
entities.summary: First Roman emperor; founder of the Principate.

name_forms.name: Octavian
name_forms.note: His name until the Senate conferred Augustus on 16 January 27 BCE. The 1911 Britannica gives 17 January.

name_forms.name: Gaius Octavius
name_forms.note: His birth name, before Caesar's will adopted him.

caveats.text: Augustus is a title the Senate voted him, not a name he was born with. He had considered Romulus and rejected it as too close to king.

entities.name: Nero
entities.summary: Fifth Roman emperor; committed suicide after being declared a public enemy.

entities.name: Nerva–Antonine Dynasty
entities.summary: Five Good Emperors; Pax Romana at its peak.
entities.date_note: Bracketed by two attested accessions and one attested murder, that of Commodus at the end of 192 CE.

entities.name: Trajan
entities.summary: Extended Rome to its greatest territorial extent.

entities.name: Hadrian
entities.summary: Consolidator emperor who built Hadrian's Wall in Britain.

entities.name: Marcus Aurelius

links.note: Insisted his adoptive brother be made coemperor, creating the first joint rule in Roman history.

entities.summary: Philosopher-emperor and author of the Meditations.

entities.name: Constantine the Great
entities.summary: Legalized Christianity; founded Constantinople.

entities.name: Byzantine Empire
entities.summary: Roman Empire's Greek-speaking continuation, based in Constantinople.
entities.date_note: The dedication of Constantinople in 330 CE is securely attested; using it as the start of a distinct empire is a choice. At least six conventions are in use, beginning at Diocletian, Constantine, Theodosius, 395, 476, Anastasius, Justinian or Heraclius. The end, 29 May 1453, is not in doubt.

alternatives.label: Byzantine begins in the 7th century
alternatives.note: The Oxford Dictionary of Byzantium uses 'late Roman' for the 4th to mid-7th centuries and reserves 'Byzantine' for what follows.

alternatives.label: Byzantine begins with the division of 395
alternatives.note: Takes the permanent administrative split after Theodosius I as the starting point.

caveats.text: Nobody in it called it Byzantine; they called it Roman. The field's own standard reference avoids the word before the 7th century.

name_forms.name: Βασιλεία τῶν Ῥωμαίων
name_forms.note: 'Empire of the Romans'. Its subjects called themselves Romans.

name_forms.name: Rhomania
name_forms.note: The everyday word for the country, as against the formal style.

entities.name: Justinian I
entities.summary: Reconquered much of the western Mediterranean; codified Roman law; built Hagia Sophia.

entities.name: Constantine XI Palaiologos
entities.summary: Last Byzantine emperor; killed defending Constantinople.

entities.name: Carolingian Empire
entities.summary: Frankish empire founded by Charlemagne; briefly reunified western Europe.

entities.name: Charlemagne
entities.summary: First Emperor of the Romans since antiquity; crowned by Pope Leo III in 800.

entities.name: France (Medieval to Modern)
entities.summary: Kingdom (later republic) of France from Hugh Capet to the present.

entities.name: Bourbon France
entities.summary: Longest-ruling French royal house; ended by the French Revolution.

entities.name: Louis XIV (Sun King)
entities.summary: Longest reign of any European monarch; built Versailles.

entities.name: French Revolution
entities.summary: Overthrew the Bourbon monarchy and reshaped modern politics.

entities.name: Napoleonic Era
entities.summary: Napoleon Bonaparte's dominance of Europe from consul to emperor and exile.

entities.name: Napoleon I
entities.summary: Emperor of the French; conquered most of continental Europe before defeat at Waterloo (1815).

entities.name: England (Medieval to Modern)
entities.summary: Kingdom of England (later Great Britain, then United Kingdom).

entities.name: Norman England
entities.summary: Norman-French dynasty founded by William the Conqueror.

entities.name: William the Conqueror
entities.summary: Conquered England at Hastings (1066).

entities.name: Plantagenet England
entities.summary: Three centuries covering Magna Carta, the first English parliaments, the Black Death, the Hundred Years' War and the Wars of the Roses.

entities.name: Tudor England
entities.summary: House that ruled England 1485–1603 including Henry VIII and Elizabeth I.

entities.name: Henry VIII
entities.summary: Broke with Rome to form the Church of England; had six wives.

entities.name: Elizabeth I
entities.summary: Presided over England's Elizabethan Golden Age of drama and exploration.

entities.name: Stuart England / Britain
entities.date_note: Stuart rule was not continuous: the monarchy was abolished from 1649 to 1660 under the Commonwealth and Protectorate, then restored. 1603-1714 is a conventional simplification that elides the interregnum.
entities.summary: Union of the English and Scottish crowns, civil war, regicide, republic, restoration and the constitutional settlement of 1688.

entities.name: Victorian Britain
entities.summary: Long reign of Queen Victoria; peak of the British Empire.

entities.name: Queen Victoria
entities.summary: Symbol of the age that bears her name; her descendants sit on many European thrones.

entities.name: Reconquista & Iberian Unification
entities.summary: The long, discontinuous Christian expansion against Muslim al-Andalus, ending in 1492 with Granada — the same year as the expulsion of the Jews and Columbus's first voyage.

entities.name: Spanish Empire
entities.date_note: 1898 ends the American and Pacific empire, which is the empire usually meant. It is not the end of Spanish overseas territory: the withdrawal from the Western Sahara in 1975-76 is the later terminus.

alternatives.label: End 1975-76 (withdrawal from the Western Sahara)
alternatives.note: The end of Spain's last significant overseas territory, and the terminus used when the second colonial empire is counted.

entities.summary: First truly global empire; the leading colonial power of the 16th century.

entities.name: Portuguese Empire
entities.date_note: Ceuta in 1415 to the Macau handover in 1999, a span of 584 years. Unusually for an empire of this size, both ends are largely uncontested.
entities.summary: Pioneered European maritime exploration; earliest and longest-lived colonial empire.

entities.name: Holy Roman Empire
entities.summary: Multi-ethnic complex of European territories notionally under an elected emperor.

name_forms.name: Sacrum Romanum Imperium
name_forms.note: 'Holy' attaches under Barbarossa's chancery in 1157; the full phrase is dated to 1184 by one account and to 1254 by others.

name_forms.name: Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation
name_forms.note: First in a document in 1474 and the official style after the Diet of Cologne in 1512, though some references still call the longer form unofficial.

entities.date_note: The 800 start is Charlemagne's coronation, a convention: contemporaries did not call it the Holy Roman Empire and the title was assembled over four centuries. 'Holy' appears in 1157, the full 'sacrum Romanum imperium' in 1184 or 1254 depending on the source, and 'of the German Nation' from 1474.

alternatives.label: Title 'sacrum Romanum imperium' standard only from 1254
alternatives.note: German History dates the expanded phrase to 1184 but its adoption as standard chancery terminology to 1254.

aliases: Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation

entities.name: Habsburg Era
entities.summary: Habsburg dynasty held the Holy Roman Emperor title almost continuously from 1438 to 1806.

entities.name: Charles V
entities.summary: Ruled an empire on which the sun never set: Spain, the HRE, Naples, the Netherlands, and Spanish America.

entities.name: The Habsburg Monarchy

name_forms.name: Austria-Hungary
name_forms.note: The dual monarchy's name after the Compromise, for the last half century of its existence.

entities.date_note: 1526 is Ferdinand I's acquisition of the Hungarian and Bohemian crowns, forming the composite realm. Habsburg rule in Austria alone goes back to 1282.
entities.summary: A composite realm assembled by marriage rather than conquest, holding together Austrians, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Croats, Romanians and Italians until nationalism pulled it apart in 1918.

entities.name: Rise of Prussia
entities.date_note: 1871 is the proclamation of the German Empire, where the story of Prussia's rise ends. Prussia itself continued as a state until 1918 and as a legal entity later still.
entities.summary: A minor Baltic state that turned military and administrative reform into great-power status, then unified Germany around itself.

entities.name: German Empire
entities.summary: Unified German state 1871–1918 under the Hohenzollerns; collapsed at the end of WWI.

entities.name: Nazi Germany
entities.summary: Totalitarian state under Hitler; started WWII in Europe and perpetrated the Holocaust.

entities.name: Post-War Germany

name_forms.name: West Germany
name_forms.note: An informal name for the same continuous state, not a predecessor of it: the GDR acceded to the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990.

name_forms.name: Deutsche Demokratische Republik
name_forms.note: A separate state until it acceded; it ceased to exist rather than merging.

entities.summary: Federal Republic of Germany from 1949 (reunified 1990).

entities.name: Viking Age
entities.summary: Norse expansion across northern Europe and the North Atlantic.

entities.name: Kievan Rus'
entities.summary: Medieval East Slavic federation; ancestor state of modern Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus.

entities.name: Grand Duchy of Moscow

alternatives.label: Britannica
alternatives.note: Britannica's own dating differs from the more commonly cited convention.

entities.date_note: 1263 is the start of Daniel's line and 1547 Ivan IV's coronation as tsar, which ends the grand-principality label. Britannica's own dating differs, c.1251-1505.
entities.summary: A minor principality under Mongol overlordship that outmanoeuvred its rivals, absorbed them, stopped paying tribute, and became the core of the Russian state.

entities.name: Tsardom of Russia
entities.summary: Russian state from Ivan IV's assumption of the tsar title to Peter I's imperial declaration.

entities.name: Ivan IV the Terrible
entities.summary: Ivan the Terrible; expanded Russia and established the Oprichnina reign of terror.

entities.name: Russian Empire
entities.summary: Multi-national empire from Peter the Great to the abdication of Nicholas II.

entities.name: Peter the Great
entities.date_note: Peter I reigned as tsar from 1682; declared himself emperor in 1721, founding the Russian Empire.
entities.summary: Westernizing tsar who founded St. Petersburg and made Russia a major European power.

entities.name: Catherine the Great
entities.summary: German-born empress who expanded Russia to the Black Sea and patronized the arts.

entities.name: Soviet Union
entities.summary: Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR); communist superpower 1922–1991.

entities.name: Vladimir Lenin
entities.date_note: Lenin led the Russian SFSR from 1917; the USSR was formally created in 1922.
entities.summary: Bolshevik leader; founded the Soviet state after the October Revolution.

entities.name: Joseph Stalin
entities.summary: Longtime dictator; industrialized the USSR at enormous human cost and led it through WWII.

entities.name: Russian Federation
entities.summary: Russian Federation from 1991 to the present.

entities.name: Scythians
entities.date_note: Re-filed from `era` to `people`: the earlier kind misdescribed what this is.

entities.name: Xiongnu Empire
entities.summary: First great nomadic empire on the Mongolian plateau.

entities.name: Kushan Empire
entities.summary: Yuezhi-descended empire linking China, India, and Rome via the Silk Road.

entities.name: First Turkic Khaganate
entities.date_note: Previously recorded as 552-744, which ran three distinct states together. The first khaganate divided into eastern and western halves around 581-603; the Tang then absorbed the east; and a second khaganate was established in 682. Only the first is dated here.

entities.name: Samanid Empire
entities.summary: A Persian revival in Bukhara and Samarkand: the dynasty under which New Persian became a literary language again, patronising Rudaki, Ferdowsi's sources and Avicenna's education.

entities.name: Mongol Empire
entities.summary: Largest contiguous empire in world history.

entities.name: Genghis Khan
entities.summary: Genghis Khan; founder of the largest contiguous land empire in world history.

entities.name: Chagatai Khanate
entities.date_note: Chagatai Khanate long outlived the unified Mongol Empire; a successor state.

entities.name: Golden Horde
entities.summary: The Jochid inheritance of the Mongol empire, ruling the western steppe and the Rus principalities. It called itself the Great State.
entities.date_note: The start depends on what is being dated -- the grant of the ulus, the western campaign, or effective independence from the Great Khan -- and specialists place it anywhere from the 1220s to the 1260s. 1502 is comparatively firm.

alternatives.label: c. 1224/25 (grant of the ulus to Jochi's line)
alternatives.note: Dates the polity from the appanage itself rather than from its independence.

alternatives.label: 1236-40 (the western campaign)
alternatives.note: Dates it from the conquest of the Rus principalities and the Kipchak steppe.

alternatives.label: c. 1260 (effective independence)
alternatives.note: The Cambridge History of the Mongol Empire treats the Horde as a separate polity only from about 1260.

caveats.text: 'Golden Horde' is a Russian coinage first attested in the 16th century, long after the fact. It called itself Ulug Ulus, 'Great State', and is also known as the ulus of Jochi.

name_forms.name: Ulug Ulus
name_forms.note: 'Great State' in Turkic, attested in the Horde's own written sources.

name_forms.name: Ulus of Jochi
name_forms.note: The Jochid inheritance, and how contemporaries placed it within the Mongol succession.

name_forms.name: Golden Horde
name_forms.note: A Russian coinage first attested in the 16th century, long after the polity it names.

name_forms.name: Kipchak Khanate
name_forms.note: After the Turkic majority of its nomadic population.

entities.name: Timurid Empire
entities.date_note: Control over Iran was loose and effectively limited to the reign of Shah Rokh; Britannica's own framing is hedged.
entities.summary: Timur's conquests were devastating and short-lived, but the dynasty he founded made Samarkand and Herat centres of astronomy, miniature painting and architecture, and produced the founder of Mughal India.

entities.name: Timur (Tamerlane)
entities.summary: Tamerlane; last of the great steppe conquerors, sacked Delhi and Damascus.

entities.name: Indus Valley Civilization
entities.summary: Bronze Age civilization along the Indus and the Ghaggar-Hakra.

name_forms.name: Harappan Civilization
name_forms.note: Named for the first site excavated, which is convention rather than precedence: Harappa was simply dug first.

name_forms.name: Sindhu-Sarasvati Civilization
name_forms.note: Ties the civilization to the Rigvedic Sarasvati. The river identification is long-standing; the renaming is contested as nationalist.

caveats.text: Which name you use is a position. 'Sindhu-Sarasvati' makes the Harappans Vedic; some historians call that hyper-nationalist, while the underlying river identification dates to 1855.

entities.date_note: Filed as a culture rather than a polity or an era: an archaeological horizon defined by material remains, whose political organisation is often the open question about it.

entities.name: Vedic Period
entities.summary: The period of the Vedic corpus in northern South Asia, dated from the texts rather than from excavation.
entities.date_note: Both ends are conventions and neither is measured. The 1500 BCE start rests on linguistic dating of the Rigveda, not on a datable event or layer. The 500 BCE end is tied to Panini and the closing of the corpus -- a fact about language; the political and economic transition to the mahajanapadas and the second urbanisation is more consistently dated around 600 BCE, and this dataset's Mahajanapadas entity begins there, so the two deliberately overlap.

alternatives.label: Ends c. 600 BCE, on the political transition
alternatives.note: The mahajanapadas, the second urbanisation, the Buddha and Mahavira.

caveats.text: Dated by comparative linguistics and internal textual evidence, not by excavation. These texts are not archaeological layers.
How Indo-Aryan speech arrived is disputed: Witzel, Parpola and Anthony argue steppe migration; Talageri, Elst and Danino argue against it. Bryant surveys both.
Three claims get merged here: language origin, material continuity, and steppe ancestry in genomes. Evidence for one is not evidence for another.

links.note: The genetic evidence, which is a separate claim from the linguistic and archaeological ones.

entities.name: Mahajanapadas (Second Urbanization)
entities.date_note: Overlaps the Later Vedic period on purpose: the second urbanisation is under way while the Vedic corpus is still closing, and the conventional Vedic end date of 500 BCE describes the language rather than the politics.
entities.summary: India's second urbanisation: sixteen or so states across the Ganges plain, some kingdoms and some republics, the setting in which Buddhism and Jainism emerged.

entities.name: Maurya Empire
entities.summary: First empire to unify most of the Indian subcontinent.

entities.name: Chandragupta Maurya
entities.summary: Founder of the Maurya Empire; unified most of the Indian subcontinent.

entities.name: Ashoka the Great
entities.date_note: Accession dates vary by source; some traditions place him from 273 BCE. Date bounds set by magnitude convention rather than from a source, pending the sourcing pass; treat the width as a floor on uncertainty.
entities.summary: After the Kalinga War, embraced Buddhism and spread it via edicts and missions.

entities.name: Shunga Empire
entities.date_note: Sources place the dynasty's end at -75 (Devabhuti's overthrow attempt) or -73 (his death).

entities.name: Satavahana Empire
entities.date_note: Founded under Simuka c. -230; imperial phase from c. -100. One of the most chronologically contested dynasties in ancient India. Britannica declines firm bounds; a Maharashtra gazetteer argues c.222 BCE-226 CE.
entities.summary: The dominant power of the Deccan between the Maurya and Gupta empires, controlling the trade that carried Roman coinage into central India.

entities.name: Indo-Greek Kingdoms
entities.summary: Greek-speaking kings ruling in Bactria and northwest India after Alexander, issuing bilingual coinage and, in Menander's case, appearing in Buddhist literature as a convert.

entities.name: Gupta Empire
entities.summary: Classical Indian empire often called the 'Golden Age of India'.

entities.name: Chola Empire
entities.summary: Great Tamil maritime empire; reached Southeast Asia.

entities.name: Delhi Sultanate
entities.summary: Muslim sultanates ruling northern India from Delhi (1206–1526).

entities.name: Mughal Empire
entities.summary: Turco-Mongol Muslim empire that ruled most of South Asia at its peak.

entities.name: Babur
entities.summary: Founder of the Mughal Empire; descendant of both Timur and Genghis Khan.

entities.name: Akbar the Great
entities.summary: Great Mughal emperor; expanded the empire and pursued religious tolerance.

entities.name: Shah Jahan
entities.summary: Built the Taj Mahal.

entities.name: Aurangzeb
entities.summary: Last of the six great Mughals; his overexpansion set the stage for imperial decline.

entities.name: Maratha Confederacy
entities.summary: The power that broke Mughal dominance in the Deccan and governed much of the subcontinent through a confederacy of chiefs, until the British defeated it in three wars.

entities.name: Sikh Empire
entities.summary: Ranjit Singh's state in Punjab, which absorbed Kashmir and Peshawar, kept the British at the Sutlej for a generation, and fell within a decade of his death.

entities.name: British Raj
entities.summary: Direct British Crown rule of India, 1858–1947.

entities.name: Post-Independence South Asia
entities.summary: Post-1947 independent states of the subcontinent.

entities.name: Funan
entities.date_note: Funan is what Chinese sources called it; no indigenous name is attested. Whether it was a unified kingdom at all is disputed, notably by Michael Vickery, who read the Chinese accounts as describing a looser set of polities.

caveats.text: A Chinese exonym. What the polity called itself is unknown.
Its existence as a single state is questioned; the evidence may describe several polities.

entities.name: Champa
entities.date_note: Champa was a confederation of polities -- Indrapura, Amaravati, Vijaya, Kauthara, Panduranga -- rather than one continuous kingdom, and it ended in stages: Vijaya fell in 1471, Kauthara was annexed in 1653, and Panduranga in 1832, which is the conventional end date used here.

caveats.text: Usually written as one kingdom, but scholarship treats it as a confederation of polities sharing a culture.
Campā is attested as a self-designation. Lin-yi and Chiêm Thành are Chinese and Vietnamese names for it.

entities.name: Khmer Empire (Angkor)
entities.summary: Southeast Asia's greatest classical empire. Built Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom.
entities.date_note: Dated from the consecration of Jayavarman II in 802 to the Ayutthayan capture of Angkor in 1431. Both ends are conventional markers: Khmer kingship neither began nor ended in a single year.

entities.name: Suryavarman II
entities.summary: Built Angkor Wat.

entities.name: Jayavarman VII
entities.summary: Built Angkor Thom and the Bayon.

entities.name: Vietnam (dynastic)
entities.summary: Independent Vietnamese states from the end of Chinese rule to the abdication of the last emperor.
entities.date_note: A container, not a polity. It previously stood as a single entity named Đại Việt covering 939-1804, which was wrong twice over: it flattened eight dynasties into one node, and Đại Việt was not the state's name for most of that time. The name applied 1054-1400 and 1428-1804; in between the state was Đại Cồ Việt, then Đại Ngu, then a Ming province.

name_forms.name: Đại Việt
name_forms.note: The name in two separate stretches, 1054-1400 and 1428-1804 -- not continuously.

name_forms.name: Đại Ngu
name_forms.note: The Hồ dynasty's name for the state.

name_forms.name: Đại Việt, 939-1804
name_forms.note: This dataset's earlier single span. The name did not apply before 1054 and lapsed twice.

name_forms.name: Siam
name_forms.note: The name outsiders used. Not the kingdom's name for itself.

entities.name: Srivijaya
entities.summary: Sumatran maritime empire that dominated the Malacca Strait.
entities.date_note: Srivijaya was not identified as a polity until 1918, when George Cœdès reconstructed it from Chinese accounts and inscriptions. Its nature is still argued -- thalassocracy, mandala, or a looser arrangement -- and even its capital is unsettled, with Palembang the usual candidate. Treat the span as the period the reconstruction covers, not as a reign-list.

caveats.text: A modern scholarly reconstruction from fragmentary evidence, not a state that named itself in surviving documents of its own.

entities.name: Majapahit Empire
entities.summary: Javanese thalassocracy at Southeast Asia's peak of classical influence.
entities.date_note: Founded 1293 after the Yuan expedition was repelled. The 1527 end is conventional, tied to Demak's conquest of Kediri; a chronogram gives 1478, and recent work dates the actual collapse to 1513-1528.

entities.name: Dutch East Indies
entities.date_note: This is the state colony, not the company. The Dutch East India Company's charter lapsed on 31 December 1799 and its possessions were nationalised, so the period beginning in 1800 is by definition not company rule. Direct Dutch administration was interrupted by French and British control from 1806 to 1816.

alternatives.label: End 1945 (Indonesian proclamation of independence)
alternatives.note: Indonesia dates independence from the 1945 proclamation; 1949 is the year the Netherlands recognised it.

caveats.text: The identifier says East India Company, but the company was wound up before this period begins. Company rule is a separate, earlier thing.

name_forms.name: Indonesia
name_forms.note: The successor state, proclaimed in 1945 and recognised by the Netherlands in 1949.

entities.name: Republic of Indonesia
entities.date_note: Independence was proclaimed on 17 August 1945; the Netherlands did not recognise it until the Hague agreement of 1949. Both dates are defensible and the choice between them is a political question, not a factual one.

alternatives.label: 1949, Dutch recognition
alternatives.note: The date the former colonial power accepted.

entities.summary: Southeast Asian archipelagic republic; world's fourth-most-populous country.

entities.name: Carthaginian Empire
entities.summary: Phoenician-founded maritime empire of the western Mediterranean.
entities.date_note: Founded from Tyre; the traditional date is 814 BCE and archaeology converges on the late ninth century. Punic is a modern term for the western Phoenicians rather than an ancient distinction the sources themselves draw.

caveats.text: Punic and Phoenician are a modern scholarly split, not one the ancient sources make consistently.

entities.name: Hannibal Barca (general)
entities.summary: Carthaginian general; crossed the Alps with elephants and terrorized Roman Italy for 15 years.

entities.name: Ghana Empire

name_forms.name: Wagadu
name_forms.note: What its own people called it. 'Ghana' was the title of its ruler.

caveats.text: The Ghana Empire lay in what is now southeastern Mauritania and western Mali, about 400 miles from the modern Republic of Ghana, which took the name in 1957.

entities.summary: Sahelian trading empire, unrelated to the modern nation of Ghana.

entities.name: Mali Empire
entities.summary: West African empire; the world's largest gold source in the 14th century.

entities.name: Sundiata Keita
entities.summary: Founder of the Mali Empire; hero of the Epic of Sundiata.

entities.name: Mansa Musa
entities.summary: Historically wealthiest ruler; famous 1324 hajj to Mecca.

entities.name: Songhai Empire
entities.summary: Largest state in West African history; overthrown by a Moroccan invasion in 1591.

caveats.text: The Benin Empire was in southern Nigeria, not the modern Republic of Benin. That country, formerly Dahomey, is named for the Bight of Benin.

entities.name: Oyo Empire
entities.summary: Yoruba cavalry empire that dominated the slave-trading coast before collapsing into civil wars.

entities.name: Swahili Coast City-States
entities.summary: Network of Indian-Ocean trading cities: Kilwa, Mombasa, Zanzibar, Sofala.

entities.name: Great Zimbabwe
entities.summary: Shona kingdom in southern Africa; famed for its stone-built capital.

entities.name: Mutapa Empire

alternatives.label: New World Encyclopedia, first Mutapa state only
alternatives.note: Treats 1803-1902 as a separate second Mutapa state.

entities.date_note: The most contested dating in this dataset: three reputable sources give three incompatible ranges, and this one is corroborated only at Wikipedia tier.
entities.summary: A gold-trading state that succeeded Great Zimbabwe, dealt with Swahili and later Portuguese merchants, and was progressively undermined by them.

entities.name: Zulu Kingdom
entities.summary: South African kingdom that fiercely resisted British colonization.

entities.name: Shaka Zulu
entities.summary: Founder of the Zulu military kingdom; revolutionized African warfare.

entities.name: Mississippian Culture
entities.summary: Mound-building cultures across the American southeast and midwest. Cahokia was North America's largest pre-Columbian city.
entities.date_note: Filed as a culture rather than a polity or an era: an archaeological horizon defined by material remains, whose political organisation is often the open question about it.

entities.name: Ancestral Puebloan

name_forms.name: Anasazi
name_forms.note: Navajo, glossed as 'enemy ancestors'. Pueblo peoples have rejected it since the early 1990s, and the National Park Service dropped it.

name_forms.name: Hisatsinom
name_forms.note: The Hopi term for their own ancestors. No general self-designation for the whole culture is recoverable.

caveats.text: The National Park Service states that no one knows what these people called themselves. Every name for them is somebody else's.

entities.date_note: Filed as a culture rather than a polity or an era: an archaeological horizon defined by material remains, whose political organisation is often the open question about it.

entities.name: Haudenosaunee Confederacy

name_forms.name: Haudenosaunee
name_forms.note: 'People of the longhouse'.

name_forms.name: Iroquois
name_forms.note: A French colonial coinage with no settled etymology; the commonest derivation is a Huron term used by an enemy nation.

entities.date_note: The founding date is genuinely unresolved. The archaeological mainstream places it in the 1450s; Mann and Fields argued for 1142 from oral tradition and a solar eclipse, and drew a published rebuttal.

alternatives.label: Founded 1142 (eclipse dating)
alternatives.note: Mann and Fields, from oral tradition plus the August 1142 solar eclipse. A dedicated rebuttal disputes the method.

entities.name: Colonial North America
entities.summary: European colonial presence in North America from Columbus to the American Revolution.

entities.name: United States

name_forms.name: America
name_forms.note: Ambiguous: also the name of two continents, which is why this dataset files the country under North America rather than the reverse.

entities.summary: United States of America from independence (1776) to the present.

entities.name: Civil War & Reconstruction
entities.summary: Union defeated the Confederacy; ended slavery and reshaped the American republic.

entities.name: Olmec Civilization
entities.summary: Mother culture of Mesoamerica.

name_forms.name: Olmeca
name_forms.note: Nahuatl for 'rubber people'. The Mexica used it for the Gulf Coast inhabitants of their own time, two millennia later than this civilization.

name_forms.name: Tenocelome
name_forms.note: 'Mouth of the jaguar', proposed by some scholars to avoid the misnomer. Not widely adopted.

entities.date_note: San Lorenzo, the earliest major centre, dates to about 1150 BCE. Filed as a culture rather than a polity or an era: an archaeological horizon defined by material remains, whose political organisation is often the open question about it.

caveats.text: The name is borrowed and wrong. Hermann Beyer applied a Nahuatl word for a much later people to this culture in 1929. No self-designation survives.

entities.name: Zapotec (Monte Albán)
entities.date_note: Runs to the Spanish conquest. The often-quoted end around 800 CE is the close of Monte Alban's Classic florescence, not of the Zapotec.
entities.summary: Builders of Monte Albán, a city levelled from a mountaintop, and users of one of the earliest writing systems in the Americas.

entities.name: Teotihuacan
entities.summary: One of the largest cities in the ancient world.
entities.date_note: The city's monumental florescence. Its inhabitants' own name for it is unknown; 'Teotihuacan' is what the Mexica called the ruins centuries later.

name_forms.name: Teotihuacan
name_forms.note: Nahuatl, roughly 'birthplace of the gods', applied by the Mexica to a city already long abandoned.

entities.name: Maya Civilization

caveats.text: The Maya never formed a single unified empire. They were dozens of independent city-states sharing a culture, script and calendar but no central authority.

entities.summary: Long-lived Mesoamerican civilization known for writing, mathematics, and monumental architecture.
entities.date_note: Filed as a culture rather than a polity or an era: an archaeological horizon defined by material remains, whose political organisation is often the open question about it.

entities.name: Classic Maya
entities.summary: Classic Maya florescence of city-states and hieroglyphic writing.

entities.name: Postclassic Maya
entities.date_note: The end depends on which ending is meant: first Spanish contact in 1519, the fall of the northern polities, or Nojpeten in 1697.

alternatives.label: Ends 1519 (first Spanish contact)
alternatives.note: Dates the end from contact rather than from the last independent Maya polity.

entities.name: Toltec Empire
entities.date_note: These dates describe the archaeological horizon centred on Tula. Whether they describe an empire is exactly what is disputed.

caveats.text: Historicists hold that Tula supported a real Toltec state. Sceptics hold that 'Toltec' is substantially a Mexica retrospective ideal. Unresolved.

entities.summary: A central Mexican power at Tula that later Mesoamericans, the Aztecs above all, treated as the model of civilisation and claimed descent from.

entities.name: Purépecha Empire

name_forms.name: Tarascan
name_forms.note: A Spanish-era name of disputed and possibly disparaging origin.

entities.date_note: Founded by Tariacuri with a capital at Patzcuaro around 1300; some sources give 1325.
entities.summary: The Aztecs' most effective rival, never conquered by them, and the only Mesoamerican state working metal for tools and weapons at scale.

entities.name: Aztec Empire

name_forms.name: Mexica
name_forms.note: What the people called themselves, more precisely Culhua-Mexica.

name_forms.name: Excan Tlatoloyan
name_forms.note: The Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, which is what the polity actually was.

name_forms.name: Aztec
name_forms.note: Popularised as a civilizational label by Humboldt in the 19th century; never a general self-designation.

entities.date_note: The Triple Alliance was formed in 1428 under Itzcoatl against Azcapotzalco, and fell with Tenochtitlan on 13 August 1521.

caveats.text: 'Aztec Empire' is a 19th-century construct for what was an alliance of three city-states. Its people were Mexica.

entities.summary: Mexica Triple Alliance dominating central Mexico until Spanish conquest.

entities.name: Itzcoatl
entities.date_note: Itzcoatl began his reign in 1427; the Triple Alliance was founded in 1428.

entities.name: Moctezuma II
entities.summary: Aztec emperor at the time of the Spanish conquest.

entities.name: Viceroyalty of New Spain
entities.summary: Spanish colonial viceroyalty covering Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean.

entities.name: Mexico (independent)
entities.summary: Independent Mexico from 1821 to the present.

entities.name: Norte Chico / Caral
entities.summary: Oldest known civilization in the Americas.

name_forms.name: Caral
name_forms.note: Often named for its largest excavated site.

entities.date_note: Monumental construction in the third millennium BCE, established by a radiocarbon programme published in Nature. Filed as a culture rather than a polity or an era: an archaeological horizon defined by material remains, whose political organisation is often the open question about it.

entities.name: Chavín
entities.date_note: Filed as a culture rather than a polity or an era: an archaeological horizon defined by material remains, whose political organisation is often the open question about it.

entities.name: Moche
entities.date_note: Britannica gives the 1st to 8th century CE; the dataset previously ended this a century early. Filed as a culture rather than a polity or an era: an archaeological horizon defined by material remains, whose political organisation is often the open question about it.

entities.name: Nazca
entities.date_note: Filed as a culture rather than a polity or an era: an archaeological horizon defined by material remains, whose political organisation is often the open question about it.

entities.name: Inca Empire
entities.summary: Largest pre-Columbian empire; stretched ~4,000 km along the Andes.

name_forms.name: Tawantinsuyu
name_forms.note: Quechua for 'the four regions together'.

name_forms.name: Inca
name_forms.note: Properly a ruler's title, extended by convention to the whole state and its people.

entities.date_note: 1438 is the earliest date confidently assignable to imperial history, when Pachacuti took the throne.

caveats.text: 'Inca' was the title of the ruler and his class, perhaps 40,000 people. It now names an empire of millions.

entities.name: Pachacuti
entities.summary: Ninth Sapa Inca; transformed a small Andean state into an empire.

entities.name: Atahualpa
entities.summary: Last independent Sapa Inca; captured and executed by Pizarro.

entities.name: Marajoara Culture
entities.date_note: Filed as a culture rather than a polity or an era: an archaeological horizon defined by material remains, whose political organisation is often the open question about it.

entities.name: Aboriginal Australia
entities.summary: One of the longest continuous cultural traditions in human history.
entities.date_note: The 65 ka arrival rests on optically stimulated luminescence at Madjedbebe, well beyond the radiocarbon range. 1788 is a colonial boundary, not an end: Aboriginal cultures and traditions continue to the present.

entities.name: Colonial Australia
entities.summary: British colonial period in Australia, 1788–1901.

entities.name: Commonwealth of Australia
entities.summary: Federated Commonwealth of Australia from 1901.

entities.name: Lapita Culture
entities.summary: An ancestral Austronesian seafaring culture that spread from the Bismarck Archipelago into Remote Oceania.
entities.date_note: The Bismarck start is 3450-3350 cal BP and the Tonga/Samoa end is 2703-2683 cal BP. Marine-shell reservoir corrections are central to this chronology. Filed as a culture rather than a polity or an era: an archaeological horizon defined by material remains, whose political organisation is often the open question about it.

alternatives.label: Earlier shell-inclusive start
alternatives.note: Shell-inclusive dates can extend the start to about 3550 cal BP after reservoir correction.

alternatives.label: Later emergence, c. 3300-3200 cal BP
alternatives.note: Kirch and others hold the Bismarck dates are no earlier than 3200 BP.

caveats.text: When Lapita begins is unresolved across roughly three centuries: Bayesian models give 3535-3234 cal BP, others no earlier than 3200.

entities.name: Saudeleur Dynasty (Nan Madol)
entities.summary: Built the megalithic city of Nan Madol on Pohnpei.

entities.name: Polynesian Voyaging & Settlement
entities.summary: A rapid expansion from West to East Polynesia that reached remote islands, including Aotearoa, in the late thirteenth century.
entities.date_note: A review of 1,434 radiocarbon dates supports 1025-1120 CE for East Polynesian settlement and 1230-1280 CE for Aotearoa, with modelled Rapa Nui about 1200 CE.

alternatives.label: Long chronology
alternatives.note: Earlier shell-inclusive chronologies placed the eastern expansion as early as 300 CE, but are superseded by short-lived samples.

entities.name: Kingdom of Hawaii
entities.summary: Unified Hawaiian Kingdom under the Kamehameha dynasty until US annexation in 1898.

entities.name: Kamehameha I
entities.summary: Warrior chief who unified the Hawaiian Islands into a single kingdom.

entities.name: Māori Aotearoa
entities.summary: Māori settlement and society of New Zealand before 1840.

entities.name: New Zealand (post-Waitangi)
entities.summary: Post-Treaty-of-Waitangi Aotearoa/New Zealand.

entities.name: Late Bronze Age Collapse
entities.summary: Systemic collapse of Mediterranean and Near Eastern civilizations c. 1200 BCE.

entities.name: Axial Age
entities.summary: Concurrent religious and philosophical revolutions: Buddha, Confucius, Zoroaster, Hebrew prophets, Greek philosophers.

entities.name: Black Death
entities.summary: Bubonic plague pandemic that killed 30–60% of Europe's population and swept Asia and North Africa.

entities.name: Age of Exploration / Age of Sail

name_forms.name: Age of Discovery
name_forms.note: A discovery only from the European end. The dataset prefers Age of Sail, which describes the technology rather than assigning a viewpoint.

caveats.text: 'Discovery' presumes whose knowledge counts as new. The places discovered were, without exception, already inhabited.

entities.summary: European maritime exploration and colonial expansion, roughly Columbus to Napoleon.

entities.name: Columbus reaches the Americas
entities.summary: Christopher Columbus's first landfall in the Bahamas; opened sustained contact between the Old World and the Americas.

entities.name: World War I
entities.summary: World War I — the first industrialized total war; ended four empires.

entities.name: World War II
entities.summary: World War II — the deadliest conflict in human history; ended with the atomic bombings of Japan.

entities.name: Cold War
entities.summary: US–USSR geopolitical rivalry, 1947–1991; defined the second half of the 20th century.

entities.name: The Renaissance
entities.summary: European cultural, artistic, and intellectual rebirth beginning in Italy and radiating outward; recovery of Greco-Roman texts; humanism.

entities.name: Italian Renaissance
entities.summary: Florentine, Venetian, and Roman flowering; Petrarch, Dante, Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael.

entities.name: Northern Renaissance
entities.summary: Renaissance north of the Alps: Erasmus, Dürer, van Eyck, printing revolution.

entities.name: The Reformation
entities.summary: Religious and political upheaval that fractured Latin Christendom, triggered by Luther's Ninety-Five Theses and ended by the Peace of Westphalia.

name_forms.name: Protestant Reformation
name_forms.note: Names the movement by its outcome and from one side; Catholic writing long preferred 'Protestant revolt'.

entities.name: Martin Luther (theologian)
entities.summary: German monk whose Ninety-Five Theses (1517) launched the Protestant Reformation.

entities.name: Thirty Years' War
entities.summary: Devastating pan-European religious and political war ending with the Peace of Westphalia.

entities.name: Scientific Revolution
entities.summary: Emergence of modern science: Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, Newton. Overturned Aristotelian and Ptolemaic worldviews.

entities.name: The Enlightenment
entities.summary: Intellectual movement emphasizing reason, individual liberty, and skepticism of tradition; foundation of modern democratic thought.

entities.name: Industrial Revolution
entities.summary: Transition from agrarian and craft economies to mechanized industry, beginning in Britain and spreading globally. Steam power, textiles, railways.

entities.name: Second Industrial Revolution
entities.summary: Steel, electricity, chemicals, internal combustion, mass production; the age of Edison, Tesla, Ford.

entities.name: Scramble for Africa
entities.summary: European colonial partition of Africa, formalized by the Berlin Conference (1884–85).

entities.name: Berlin Conference
entities.summary: European powers agreed rules for the partition of Africa; no African representatives present.

entities.name: Decolonization
entities.summary: Dissolution of European colonial empires after WWII; independence for most of Africa, Asia, and the Pacific.

entities.name: Napoleonic Wars
entities.summary: Series of conflicts pitting Napoleon's France against shifting European coalitions. Reshaped the continent.

entities.name: Battle of Austerlitz
entities.summary: Napoleon's masterpiece; defeat of the Third Coalition (Austria and Russia).

entities.name: Battle of Trafalgar
entities.summary: Nelson's decisive naval victory over the Franco-Spanish fleet; secured British naval supremacy for a century.

entities.name: Battle of Waterloo
entities.summary: Napoleon's final defeat at the hands of Wellington and Blücher; end of the Napoleonic era.

entities.name: Assassination of Julius Caesar
entities.summary: Caesar assassinated on the Ides of March, 44 BCE, by a conspiracy of senators.
entities.date_note: 15 March 44 BCE. Attested by contemporaries and among the most securely dated events in Roman history.

entities.name: Battle of Actium
entities.summary: Octavian's naval victory over Antony and Cleopatra; effective end of the Republic.
entities.date_note: 2 September 31 BCE, securely attested.

entities.name: Korean War
entities.summary: First major hot conflict of the Cold War; UN-backed South Korea vs. Chinese/Soviet-backed North.

entities.name: Vietnam War
entities.summary: Prolonged conflict ending with North Vietnamese victory and reunification.

entities.name: Cuban Missile Crisis
entities.summary: Thirteen-day nuclear standoff between the US and USSR over Soviet missiles in Cuba — the closest the Cold War came to nuclear war.

entities.name: Apollo 11 Moon Landing
entities.summary: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first humans to walk on the Moon (20 July 1969).

entities.name: Fall of the Berlin Wall
entities.summary: Symbolic end of the Cold War division of Europe; East Germans crossed freely on 9 November 1989.

entities.name: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
entities.summary: Formal end of the USSR on 26 December 1991; 15 successor republics.

entities.name: September 11 Attacks
entities.summary: Coordinated al-Qaeda attacks on the United States; triggered the War on Terror.

entities.name: War on Terror
entities.summary: US-led military campaign following 9/11; wars in Afghanistan (2001–2021) and Iraq (2003–2011).
entities.date_note: Declared and led by the United States; NATO invoked Article 5 for the only time in its history, so the campaigns were multinational. Filed under both.

entities.name: Global Financial Crisis
entities.summary: Worldwide financial crisis triggered by the US subprime mortgage collapse; deepest downturn since the Great Depression.

entities.name: COVID-19 Pandemic
entities.summary: Global pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2; declared over as an emergency by the WHO in May 2023.

entities.name: Neolithic Transition
entities.summary: Independent, and largely unconscious, transitions to farming in at least seven regions. A process of millennia, not an event.
entities.date_note: NOT A REVOLUTION, despite the name it is still filed under. The dominant model is protracted and geographically autonomous: domestication took on the order of 4,000 years, happened independently at several foci, and was largely unconscious rather than invented. The field has largely replaced Childe's 'Neolithic Revolution' with 'Neolithic transition' for that reason. The end date is diachronous and runs past the Neolithic label itself, because Eastern North America domesticates thousands of years after the Fertile Crescent.

alternatives.label: Rapid, conscious, core-area domestication
alternatives.note: Abbo and Gopher argue for a fast deliberate process in one core area.

caveats.text: Not a revolution and not an event: the transition took millennia, and foraging and farming coexisted throughout much of it.
How many independent centres exist is unsettled: Harlan counted 6, Vavilov 12, Purugganan and Fuller 24.
Called a Transition here rather than a Revolution: the process took roughly four thousand years in Southwest Asia, which is not what the word revolution conveys.

name_forms.name: Neolithic Revolution
name_forms.note: Childe's label, and the famous one. It implies a speed this dataset's own entities contradict.

entities.name: Tiberius
entities.summary: Augustus's stepson and successor.

entities.name: Caligula
entities.summary: Notorious for cruelty; assassinated by the Praetorian Guard.

name_forms.name: Gaius
name_forms.note: His actual name: Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus Germanicus.

name_forms.name: Caligula
name_forms.note: 'Little boot', a soldiers' nickname from his childhood in camp. The sources say he disliked it, and it is how history knows him.

entities.name: Claudius
entities.summary: Conquered Britain (43 CE).

entities.name: Galba
entities.date_note: Galba was proclaimed emperor in 68, before the Year of the Four Emperors year (69).

entities.name: Vespasian
entities.summary: Founded the Flavian dynasty; began the Colosseum.

entities.name: Titus
entities.summary: Vesuvius erupted (79 CE) during his reign; destroyed Jerusalem (70 CE).

entities.name: Lucius Verus
entities.summary: Co-emperor with Marcus Aurelius.

links.note: Equal in constitutional status but not in authority: equal in all respects except pontifex maximus, which Marcus kept.

entities.name: Commodus
entities.summary: Son of Marcus Aurelius; his reign is often cited as the start of Rome's decline.

entities.name: Pescennius Niger
entities.date_note: Rival claimant into 194, after the nominal Year of Five Emperors year (193).

entities.name: Clodius Albinus
entities.date_note: Rival claimant into 197, well after the nominal 193 year.

entities.name: Severan Dynasty
entities.summary: A dynasty of provincial origin that widened citizenship, leaned openly on the army for legitimacy, and ended in the assassination that opened the third-century crisis.

entities.name: Septimius Severus
entities.summary: African-born emperor; expanded to Mesopotamia.

entities.name: Caracalla
entities.summary: Extended Roman citizenship to all free inhabitants (Constitutio Antoniniana, 212).

entities.name: Crisis of the Third Century
entities.summary: Fifty years of civil war, plague, and near-collapse.
entities.date_note: The years are attested. The label is the problem: 'crisis' asserts a coherent systemic collapse, and a substantial body of archaeological work argues the evidence does not support one empire-wide.

caveats.text: Lewitt, Witschel and others reject the total-crisis model. The name smuggles in an interpretation, which is unusual for a dating label.

entities.name: Decius
entities.summary: First empire-wide persecution of Christians.

entities.name: Valerian
entities.summary: Captured alive by the Sasanian king Shapur I.

entities.name: Aurelian
entities.summary: Restored the empire; reconquered Palmyra and the Gallic Empire.

entities.name: Carinus
entities.date_note: Carinus continued reigning into 285, one year past Diocletian's accession that starts the Dominate.

entities.name: Diocletian
entities.summary: Founded the Tetrarchy; ended the third-century crisis. Last major persecution of Christians.

entities.name: Maxentius

entities.name: Licinius
entities.summary: Co-issued the Edict of Milan (313) legalizing Christianity.

entities.name: Constantinian Dynasty
entities.date_note: Some schemes begin the dynasty at 305 rather than 306 CE, depending on whether Constantius I's accession or Constantine's acclamation is taken as the start.
entities.summary: Roman imperial dynasty led by Constantine the Great and his successors; Christianization of the Empire.

entities.name: Julian the Apostate

entities.name: Jovian
entities.date_note: Jovian's reign spilled slightly into 364, technically after Constantinian dynasty end.

entities.name: Valentinianic & Theodosian Dynasties

entities.name: Valens

entities.name: Theodosius I the Great

entities.name: Valentinian III (West)

entities.name: Heraclius

entities.name: Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus

entities.name: Basil II the Bulgar-Slayer
entities.summary: Presided over Byzantium at its medieval peak.

entities.name: Romanos IV Diogenes

entities.name: Alexios I Komnenos

entities.name: Manuel II Palaiologos

entities.name: Empress Dowager Lü

entities.name: Demetrius I of Bactria

entities.name: Menander I 'Soter'
entities.summary: Greatest Indo-Greek king; the Buddhist king Milinda of the Milindapañha dialogues.

name_forms.name: Menander I Soter
name_forms.note: 'Saviour', from his coinage.

name_forms.name: Milinda
name_forms.note: His name in the Pali Milindapanha, where he debates a Buddhist monk and converts. He is remembered in two traditions under two names.

entities.name: Strato II
entities.summary: Last known Indo-Greek king; ended by Indo-Scythian conquest.

entities.summary: Founder of the imperial Gupta dynasty.

entities.name: Samudragupta
entities.summary: Warrior-emperor who conquered much of the subcontinent; commemorated in the Allahabad Prashasti inscription.

entities.name: Kumaragupta I
entities.summary: Founded the Nalanda monastic university.

entities.name: Skandagupta
entities.summary: Repelled the Hephthalite (White Hun) invasions; last of the great Guptas.

entities.name: Narasimhagupta Baladitya
entities.summary: Defeated the Hun ruler Mihirakula.

entities.name: Vishnugupta

entities.name: Harshavardhana
entities.summary: Buddhist emperor of Kannauj; his court was described by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang.

entities.name: Vijayalaya Chola

entities.name: Kulottunga I

entities.name: Pallava Dynasty

entities.name: Mahendravarman I
entities.summary: Warrior-poet-playwright; started the rock-cut temple tradition.

entities.name: Narasimhavarman I
entities.summary: Founded Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram); defeated the Chalukyas.

entities.name: Pala Empire
entities.summary: Buddhist dynasty of Bengal and Bihar; patronized Nalanda and founded Vikramashila.

entities.name: Gopala
entities.summary: Founder of the Pala dynasty; elected by a council of chiefs.

entities.name: Dharmapala

entities.name: Devapala
entities.summary: Peak of Pala power.

entities.name: Rashtrakuta Dynasty
